chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
title: A hangout where musicians get in free
summary: He says musicians drop in free, recalling Roosevelt fake musicians with closed cases, and wanting a hangout like the Green Mill.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Just for the historic record, Willie was here last night -
He usually comes in every Sunday evening.
Do you have a lot of musicians of that caliber coming in here on their off nights just to hang out?

Yeah, yeah. There were several guitarists last night, Henry Johnson among them. They come in and we let the musicians in free, because, you know, we’re one big family. Of course there’s some people, like at Roosevelt, they used to have people come up to the sessions every week with their cases, and they’d never open up the cases to play, and

they’d always leave with a couple of chicks trailing ‘em, you know. I said, “I bet they don’t even have horns in there.” So when they come to the door and they say “we’re musicians” we have to sort of try and verify that some way. “Here’s my union card.” I said, “A union card doesn’t mean you’re a musician. It means you gave them some money.” Yeah.
Well, what the hell. It’s a hangout. We were trying to make it a hangout like the Green Mill is.

But those places - now back to that - there are very few places that still exist. I remember moving back from Europe and I moved down to San Diego. There’s the Blue Parrot, of course some of the places, and that was kind of the end of that era, where musicians used to go and hang out afterwards. And just cause, you know, unless you’re on the bandstand together you really didn’t see each other that much, or rarely. And so those places tend to have really gone by the by, whereas here it seems like you’ve carried, you are carrying on an important tradition there.
